claims.text: The free-standing T-bar row uses a barbell anchored in a landmine at one end, loaded with plates at the other, with a close-grip V-handle hooked under the bar about 8-10 inches from the plates.

quotes.text: Secure a barbell to a landmine attachment and load the free end of the bar with weight plates.
Hook a chinning triangle or close-grip dual handle about eight to 10 inches from the weight plate so it is facing upward.

claims.text: Stand over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent, and hinge forward at the hips.

quotes.text: Stand over the barbell with your feet about shoulder-width apart, bend your knees slightly, and hinge at the hips to lean forward.

claims.text: Hold the handle with both hands, brace, and keep the back straight with the chest parallel to the floor.

quotes.text: Grab the handle with both hands, engage your core, and keep your back straight so your chest is parallel to the floor.

claims.text: Pull toward the lower chest by pulling the shoulder blades back and driving the elbows back, then squeeze at the top.

quotes.text: Pull the barbell toward your lower chest by retracting your shoulder blades and driving your elbows back.
Contract your back muscles at the top of the movement.

claims.text: Lower slowly to the start, keeping tension in the back.

quotes.text: Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position while maintaining tension throughout your back muscles.

claims.text: The hands on the handle are turned inward (palms facing each other).

quotes.text: Grasp the handle with both hands turned inward
quotes.where: How To Do T-Bar Rows At Home

claims.text: Rounding the back is one of the most common T-bar row mistakes; it strains the spinal erectors and raises the chance of a lower-back injury. Keep the trunk braced and use a load you can handle.

quotes.text: Lifters round their backs is one of the most common mistakes I see when training.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

quotes.text: this loss of proper form can place a tremendous strain on your spinal erectors and ramp up your chances of suffering a lower-back injury. Keep your core engaged and use an appropriate load for your strength levels.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

claims.text: Don’t swing from rep to rep; hold the squeeze at the top.

quotes.text: Avoid swinging from one rep to the next by holding the contraction at the top.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Using Momentum

claims.text: Use the full range: don’t stop halfway down.

quotes.text: Don’t lower the weight halfway down, and do yourself a favor by executing the full repetitions to reap the most muscle-building rewards.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Not Completing the Full Range of Motion

claims.text: The T-bar row mainly works the lats, rhomboids and erector spinae, with the biceps and rear delts supporting.

quotes.text: The T-bar row primarily engages the back muscles—the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and erector spinae. Meanwhile, your biceps and rear deltoids play supporting roles.
quotes.where: Muscles Worked by the T-Bar Row

claims.text: Without a chest pad, the lower back has to work much harder to hold the position.

quotes.text: However, when your chest isn’t supported, there are much higher demands on your lower back to maintain proper form.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

claims.text: On the chest-supported T-bar machine, set the foot plate so the sternum sits at the end of the pad.

quotes.text: Set the foot plate so that your sternum is at the end of the support bench.

claims.text: Beginners start light and focus on form, adding weight gradually as strength and technique improve.

quotes.text: Beginners can safely perform the T-Bar row by starting with light weights and focusing on proper form. Gradually increasing the weight as strength and technique improve will help prevent injury and lead to progress.

claims.text: Add load in small steps (2-10%) only once the target reps are exceeded by one or two.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s up and 1-2 s down, with a short hold at the top and a slow lowering.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC).
Avoid swinging from one rep to the next by holding the contraction at the top.

claims.text: Heavy lifting with a held breath (Valsalva) drives blood pressure very high.

quotes.text: It was concluded that when healthy young subjects perform weight-lifting exercises the mechanical compression of blood vessels combines with a potent pressor response and a Valsalva response to produce extreme elevations in blood pressure.

claims.text: In a lab comparison, the standing bent-over row gave the largest lumbar spine load of three rows; the free-standing T-bar row is also a standing bent-over row, so this likely applies (inferred, not measured on the T-bar).

quotes.text: The standing bent-over row produced large activation symmetrically across the back but produced the largest lumbar spine load.

claims.text: Back pain with weakness or numbness in both legs, or loss of feeling around the genitals, needs 999; pain not better after a few weeks needs a GP.

quotes.text: Call 999 or go to A&E if:
pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus
See a GP if:
it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks

claims.text: Wrap the thumbs around the handle.

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

claims.text: Lifting straps help on heavy rows when the grip limits the back work.

quotes.text: Lifting straps can aid your grip strength during heavy rows.

plate.viewWhy: The chest-parallel back, the hinge and the handle path to the lower chest are front-to-back (c2, c3, c4); the census draws it side.
plate.equipment: Landmine rig: a barbell pinned at a floor pivot behind the lifter, plates on the free end, a V-handle hooked under the bar 8-10 inches from the plates (c1). Needs the landmine composer (census gap).
plate.start: Standing over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent (c2), hips hinged, back straight, chest parallel to the floor (c3), arms straight down to the handle.
plate.end: Same back angle (c3); elbows driven back, handle at the lower chest, shoulder blades pulled back (c4).

checkpoints.label: Chest parallel
checkpoints.what: Back straight, chest level with the floor.

checkpoints.label: Soft knees
checkpoints.what: Knees slightly bent, hips hinged back.

checkpoints.label: Elbows back
checkpoints.what: Elbows drive back, handle to the lower chest.

mistake.what: Rounded back: the spine bends forward over the bar.
mistake.why: Named one of the most common T-bar mistakes, straining the spinal erectors and raising lower-back injury risk (c7) on an unsupported lift that already loads the lower back (c11, c17).

plate.variantLine: Drawn: the free-standing (landmine) T-bar with a V-handle (c1). The library also allows a chest-supported T-bar machine: there the foot plate is set so the sternum is at the end of the pad (c12) and the lower back works less (c11). Claims c4-c10, c13-c16, c19-c20 hold for both; c2, c3, c7, c17 and the back box are for the free-standing version.

grip.type: Neutral: palms facing each other on a V-handle.
grip.handContact: Handle across the base of the fingers and top of the palm (pull archetype); straps allowed on heavy sets.
grip.wrist: Straight in line with the forearm (pull archetype range); not curled.

setup.step: Barbell in a landmine, plates on the free end.
Hook a V-handle under the bar about 8-10 inches from the plates.
Stand over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent.
Hinge until the chest is level with the floor; grab the handle, palms facing.

posture.point: Back straight, chest parallel to the floor.
Shoulder blades pull back as the elbows drive back.
Hold the squeeze at the top; no swinging.

handlingMistakes.fix: Brace and use a lighter load.
Hold the squeeze at the top of each rep.
Lower until the arms are straight.

rows.where: Middle and sides of the back
rows.means: Usually means the lats and upper back are doing the rowing.
Usually means it is holding the bent-over position, which is expected without a chest pad.

rows.where: Lower back pain, or pain or numbness down both legs

risks.risk: A rounded back strains the lower back and raises the chance of injury.
Without a chest pad the lower back works much harder.
Holding your breath hard on heavy reps sends blood pressure very high.

zooms.right: Palms facing on the V-handle, thumbs wrapped, wrists straight.
zooms.wrong: Wrists curled, handle sliding to the fingertips.

zooms.right: Back straight, chest level with the floor, soft knees.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary mid_back and secondary lats, biceps, rear_delts fit (c10). The library lists no stabiliser; add lower_back as a stabiliser: the anchor names the erector spinae as a primary muscle (c10), and without a chest pad the lower back works much harder (c11).
